title: Blessing children
hookLine: a parent traces a cross on a child's forehead at night

lines: LIGHTS OUT. A THUMB ON THE FOREHEAD.
cards: Lights out. The story is finished, the water glass is on the nightstand, and a small voice has asked for one more thing and been told no.
The parent leans down in the dark and, with a thumb, draws a small cross on the child's forehead. Down, then across. Sometimes with a few words, sometimes none.
The child is often half asleep and doesn't notice. Years later, that child is a teenager walking out the door with car keys, and the parent's thumb still finds the forehead on the way out.
Where does a habit like that come from? Further back than bedtime.

teach.b: Start in Mark's Gospel. People are bringing children to Jesus, and the disciples try to send them away. Jesus is indignant: let the little children come.
Then Mark slows down, in the Douay-Rheims: "And embracing them, and laying his hands upon them, he blessed them." Not a lesson. Not a test.
Arms, hands, and a blessing. Next, where the cross on the forehead comes from.
At an infant's baptism, before the water, the priest or deacon welcomes the child and traces the sign of the cross on the forehead, claiming the child for Christ.
Then the rite invites the parents and godparents to do the same. So the first cross on that forehead is made by the Church, and the next ones by the people who will raise the child.

teach.h: THE FIRST CROSS IS AT BAPTISM.
teach.b: The bedtime cross is the baptism cross, repeated. Then, the parent's part. The Church's book of blessings includes blessings that parents themselves may lead for their children.
The thumb at bedtime isn't borrowing anyone's job; it's finishing what the parents were invited to begin at the font. Last, what it's for.
Catholic parents who bless their children at night are handing them back, for the hours they can't watch over them, to the one they believe is always watching.

teach.h: THE LAST WORD OF THE DAY.
teach.b: It's also a way to end a hard day well.

teach.h: LAYING HIS HANDS UPON THEM, HE BLESSED THEM.
teach.b: Whatever the argument was about at dinner, the last word of the day is a blessing.

how: Some Catholic parents bless their children each night, or as they leave the house, by tracing a small sign of the cross on the forehead with a thumb, sometimes with holy water or a few words. The custom echoes the cross the priest, parents and godparents trace on the child's forehead at baptism.

o: he agrees the children should wait until he's finished teaching.

games.why: he's indignant with the disciples, lets the children come, and then, Mark says, "embracing them, and laying his hands upon them, he blessed them."

practice: Bring one person you love to mind, a child, a parent, a friend far away, and see their face clearly. If they're near tonight, you could ask whether they'd like a small cross on the forehead before sleep.
If you pray, trace that cross in the air toward them and ask God to keep them; if you don't, wish them well by name, slowly, with your hand resting open on your knee.

wordCard.voice: Blessing children. The Catholic custom of parents tracing the sign of the cross on a child's forehead, repeating the cross made at baptism. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the sign of the cross, the gesture a parent's thumb makes on a forehead.

carryVoice: Your line: a cross on the forehead. Down, then across, the cross first made at the font. That's today, done.
